context: Part of the creation account, in which God says "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness."
ldsInterpretation: LDS apologists highlight the plural "us" and "our" as consistent with a council of divine beings (see also Abraham 4-5, which uses "Gods" throughout the creation account), and read "image" and "likeness" as indicating humans are literally of the same kind of being as God, not merely His handiwork.

context: Within Paul's extended argument for the reality of the resurrection, he appeals to a practice among some believers of being "baptized for the dead."
ldsInterpretation: LDS apologists read this as evidence that vicarious baptism for deceased persons was practiced (or at least known and not condemned) among first-century Christians, and see it as the New Testament anchor for the LDS temple ordinance of baptism for the dead described in Doctrine and Covenants 128.

quotes.author: Tertullian
quotes.text: Tertullian confirms the practice of vicarious baptism among some Christians of his era and connects it directly to this verse.

context: The Lord calls Jeremiah to be a prophet, telling him: "Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations."
ldsInterpretation: LDS apologists read "before I formed thee" and "before thou camest forth" as indicating Jeremiah had a real, known existence and was foreordained to his mission prior to mortal conception -- consistent with the LDS doctrine of a premortal spirit existence and foreordination described in Abraham 3:22-23.

context: "Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets."
ldsInterpretation: LDS apologists cite this as describing an ongoing pattern of how God operates -- always working through living prophets -- rather than a one-time historical arrangement that ended with the biblical canon. Critics note the immediate context concerns God's judgments on ancient Israel specifically, not a general theological statement about revelation continuing indefinitely.

context: Paul tells the Thessalonians the day of Christ will not come "except there come a falling away first, and that man of sin be revealed."
ldsInterpretation: The Greek word translated "falling away," apostasia, is the direct origin of the LDS term "Great Apostasy." LDS apologists read this verse as a clear apostolic prediction that widespread doctrinal and institutional corruption would occur before the Second Coming, making a Restoration (rather than only a Reformation) necessary.

quotes.author: Cyril of Jerusalem
quotes.text: For men have fallen from the right faith... This, therefore, is the falling away.
quotes.source: Catechetical Lectures, commenting on this verse

context: Ezekiel is commanded to write on two sticks (or tablets) -- one for Judah, one for Joseph/Ephraim -- and to join them into one in his hand as a sign to the people.
ldsInterpretation: LDS apologists read the "stick of Joseph" as symbolizing the Book of Mormon (a record of a branch of the house of Joseph) becoming one with the "stick of Judah" (the Bible) in the latter days. Ezekiel's own explanation in verses 15-23 concerns the reunification of the divided kingdoms of Israel and Judah under one king, which many LDS scholars now treat as the passage's primary meaning, with the scripture-record reading held as a secondary, typological application rather than the literal, sole intent of the prophecy.

context: "And no man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron."
ldsInterpretation: LDS apologists cite this as the clearest biblical statement of the principle underlying priesthood authority: that authority to act for God must come by proper divine calling and ordination, not by self-assertion, personal study, or congregational vote alone.

context: Jesus says, "And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd."
ldsInterpretation: LDS apologists read "other sheep" as Christ's own reference to other peoples who would also receive His ministry and word -- understood in LDS theology to include the peoples described in the Book of Mormon, whom the resurrected Christ visits in 3 Nephi 15:21.
